scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

In fact, it’s *responsible*. - Skipping the joint party to see your dad alone isn’t about excluding her—it’s about **protecting yourself** in a way that aligns with your capacity to cope. You’re not "giving up" on her; you’re refusing to harm yourself further. 2. **The Guilt You’re Feeling Is Valid (But Not Justified)** - Guilt often stems from a misplaced sense of duty ("I *should* endure this for my family"). But your parents *know* about the abuse and have already expressed understanding (even if they’re hesitant). Their plea to "not give up on her" likely comes from love and fear—not from a demand that you sacrifice your well-being. - **Ask yourself:** *Would I tell my husband to endure emotional abuse for his family’s sake?* If not, why does the answer differ for yourself? 3. **The "Slippery Slope" Fear** - You might worry that skipping this party sets a precedent for future exclusions. But boundaries aren’t about punishment—they’re about **sustainability**. If you can’t attend without severe distress, it’s not a failure; it’s a sign you need to adjust expectations. - Over time, your parents may come to respect your limits if they see you’re not avoiding them but *protecting yourself*. Right now, their fear of her BPD might cloud their judgment, but their love for you is real. 4. **Honesty vs. Deception** - You’re considering a **partial truth** (coming for Dad’s birthday but not the joint party) with a plausible excuse. This is a gray area: - **Pros:** It allows you to see your dad without lying outright, and you’re not excluding him entirely. - **Cons:** It’s still a form of omission, which could feel dishonest to you (or to your parents if they notice). If you’re comfortable with the moral weight of this, it might be a bridge between your needs and your family’s expectations. - **Alternative:** If you’re open to it, you could frame it as a **logistical impossibility** (e.g., "I wish I could make it both weekends, but my husband’s work schedule only allows one trip this month"). This keeps it honest while still honoring your limits. 5. **The Long-Term Impact** - **On You:** If you attend the joint party and it triggers a meltdown, relapse into depression, or leaves you resentful, the short-term "family harmony" won’t outweigh the cost. Boundaries are about **preventing harm**, not causing it. - **On Your Parents:** They may initially feel hurt, but if they truly care about you, they’ll eventually see that you’re not abandoning them—you’re choosing a healthier way to be present. Their fear of her BPD might make them cling to the idea of "saving" her, but your healing is also their gift to you. - **On Your Sister:** She may feel excluded, but **you owe her nothing**. Her emotions are her responsibility, not yours. If she reacts poorly, that’s on her—not you. --- ### **Constructive Judgments** - **You’re Not the Villain Here.** Your sister’s behavior is toxic, and your parents’ fear of her complicates things, but you’re not obligated to endure abuse for their comfort. This isn’t about "winning" or "losing"—it’s about **survival**. - **Your Approach Is Ethical.** While the partial truth feels like a compromise, it’s a **pragmatic** way to honor multiple needs (your dad’s, your own, and your family’s) without causing unnecessary harm. It’s not ideal, but it’s a step toward what works for you. - **The Guilt Will Fade.** Right now, it feels overwhelming, but with time, you’ll likely realize that **you didn’t "fail" your family by prioritizing yourself**. In fact, you’re modeling healthy self-advocacy for them. --- ### **Suggestions for Moving Forward** 1. **Script a Honest (But Gentle) Explanation** If you feel comfortable, you could say something like: > *"I really wanted to be there for both of you, but this month, my mental health needs to come first. I’m coming down for Dad’s birthday because I love him, but I need to take care of myself too. I hope you understand."* This acknowledges their feelings while setting a boundary. If they push back, you can reiterate that you’ve already discussed this with them and that your well-being is non-negotiable. 2. **Prepare for Their Reaction** They might feel hurt, angry, or confused. This is normal. You can: - Validate their feelings: *"I know this might feel like I’m choosing myself over you, but it’s not. I’m choosing to be the best version of myself so I can be there for you in the future."* - Offer reassurance: *"I’m not giving up on our relationship—I’m just learning how to engage with it in a way that works for me."* 3. **Reframe the Narrative** Instead of seeing this as "skipping" the party, think of it as: - **A gift to your dad:** You’re giving him undivided attention and affection. - **A gift to yourself:** You’re modeling resilience and self-care. - **A gift to your parents:** You’re showing them that their love for you doesn’t require you to endure harm. 4. **Consider a Gradual Approach** If this feels too abrupt, you could start by **reducing your time at the joint party** (e.g., arriving late, leaving early) to ease into smaller boundaries. This might help your parents adjust to the idea without feeling blindsided. 5. **Lean on Your Support System** - Your husband: Does he support your boundaries? If not, this is a conversation you two need to have. - Therapist: Bring this up in session to process the guilt and strategize. - Trusted friends/family: Sometimes an outside perspective can help you see the situation more clearly. --- ### **Final Thought** You’re at a crossroads where **love and self-preservation collide**. The fact that you’re even asking this question shows how deeply you care—not just about your family, but about *yourself*. That’s a strength, not a flaw. **You are allowed to love your dad without loving your sister’s abuse.** You are allowed to heal without guilt. And you are allowed to ask for what you need—even if it feels like you’re asking for too much. This isn’t about being "right" or "wrong." It’s about **being true to yourself** in a way that honors your values, your healing, and your relationships—even when it’s messy. You’re doing the hard but necessary work of setting boundaries, and that takes courage. Trust that your parents, in time, will see that you’re not abandoning them—you’re choosing a life that includes them *and* you.
